idiom_name: std::variant recursion + std::visit over an overload set
implementation_notes: The modern C++ default: node kinds are plain structs in a recursive std::variant, children are held through std::unique_ptr, and each operation is one std::visit with an overload set of lambdas. std::visit refuses to compile a callable that cannot be invoked for every alternative, which recovers exhaustiveness that the virtual form only gets from discipline - but the alternative list is fixed, so a grammar that third parties extend cannot use it.
pitfalls: A variant cannot contain itself directly: recursive alternatives need std::unique_ptr (or a recursive_wrapper), or the type is incomplete.
std::visit cannot forward extra arguments, so the context must be stored in the visitor object or captured by a generic lambda.
A variant is as large as its largest alternative and never allocates for small nodes, so mixing a big nonterminal with a small literal wastes memory in every node.

variants.name: Abstract base class with virtual eval
variants.idiom_name: abstract class Expr declaring virtual eval(const Context&), one class per rule
variants.implementation_notes: The classic GoF shape in C++: an abstract Expr declaring pure virtual eval(const Context&), one derived class per grammar rule, children in std::unique_ptr<Expr>. It keeps the node set open - a grammar can be extended from another translation unit or plugin - at the cost of a vtable lookup and a separate allocation per node. Production compiler front ends still use this shape for exactly the reason the closed variant form cannot: new node kinds arrive without editing the evaluator.
pitfalls: Copying through the base class slices; a virtual clone() is required if nodes must be copied.
Every node is a separate allocation plus a vptr load per evaluation - the cost std::variant removes in exchange for a closed type set.
Destructors must be virtual or deleting through a base pointer is undefined behaviour.
